On infinite families of [Pn][P_{n}]-irregular graphs

Tatiana Dovzhenok ††thanks: Corresponding author. E-mail: t.dovzhenok@mail.ru Affiliation: Research Laboratory ‘‘Mathematics of Hybrid Intelligence Systems’’, Francisk Skorina Gomel State University, Gomel, 246028, Belarus    Ilya Lukashenko Affiliation: Faculty of Information Technologies and Control, Belarusian State University of Informatics and Radioelectronics, Minsk, 220013, Belarus Affiliation: Research Laboratory ‘‘Algebra and Geometry of Complex Systems’’, Francisk Skorina Gomel State University, Gomel, 246028, Belarus    Andrei Mikhalev Affiliation: Research Laboratory ‘‘Algebra and Geometry of Complex Systems’’, Francisk Skorina Gomel State University, Gomel, 246028, Belarus    Yahor Filiuta Affiliation: Research Laboratory ‘‘Algebra and Geometry of Complex Systems’’, Francisk Skorina Gomel State University, Gomel, 246028, Belarus
Abstract

This paper presents the first systematic study of [F][F]-irregular graphs, a concept that parallels classical FF-irregularity. For a fixed graph FF, a graph GG is [F][F]-irregular if the numbers of its induced subgraphs isomorphic to FF containing a given vertex are pairwise distinct for all vertices of GG. We prove that there exist infinitely many [Pn][P_{n}]-irregular graphs for any path PnP_{n} of order n≥3n\geq 3. We establish that a non-trivial [P3][P_{3}]-irregular graph of order kk exists if and only if k≥7k\geq 7. Finally, we propose the Strong Conjecture on [F][F]-irregular graphs.

Keywords: induced subgraphs, induced paths, graph irregularity, [F][F]-degree of a vertex, [F][F]-irregular graph, Strong Conjecture on [F][F]-irregular graphs.

1 Introduction

While regular graphs are central to algebraic and structural graph theory, vertex-distinguishing problems have motivated multiple paradigms of irregularity [1]. In what follows, we exclusively consider simple, finite, and undirected graphs. Since no non-trivial graph can have pairwise distinct vertex degrees, a core challenge is to define generalized degree concepts that distinguish all vertices of the graph.

One such direction originates from the seminal work of Chartrand, Holbert, Oellermann, and Swart [2], who associated each vertex vv of a graph GG with the number of its subgraphs isomorphic to a fixed graph FF that contain vv. This quantity, termed the FF-degree of vv, naturally captures structural asymmetry: a graph GG is called FF-irregular if its vertices have mutually distinct FF-degrees. In [2], the authors put forward a fundamental conjecture on the existence of such graphs, motivated by their study of the cases where FF is a complete graph or a star.

Conjecture 1 (Chartrand et al. [2], 1987).

For every connected graph FF of order |F|≥3|F|\geq 3, there exists a non-trivial FF-irregular graph.

Further progress for broader classes of graphs was made only in 2024, when Dovzhenok, Filuta, and Chuhai [3] demonstrated that infinite families of FF-irregular graphs exist for all 22-connected graphs FF with minimum degree 22. In the same work, the authors proposed a significantly stronger version of Conjecture 1.

Conjecture 2 (Strong Conjecture about FF-irregular graphs, Dovzhenok et al. [3], 2024).

For every connected graph FF of order |F|≥3|F|\geq 3, there are infinitely many FF-irregular graphs.

Subsequently, Dovzhenok verified Conjecture 1 for paths [4] and confirmed Conjecture 2 for all graphs FF of diameter 2 [5].

In the present paper, in contrast to the classical setting based on ordinary subgraphs, we focus on irregularity through the lens of induced subgraphs. This approach was originally suggested by Ali, Chartrand, and Zhang in [1].

Definition 1.

Let FF and GG be graphs. The induced FF-degree (or simply [F][F]-degree) of a vertex vv in GG is the number of induced subgraphs of GG that are isomorphic to FF and contain vv. A graph GG is [F][F]-irregular if the [F][F]-degrees of its vertices are pairwise distinct.

Unlike ordinary subgraphs, which are preserved under edge addition, their induced counterparts are highly sensitive to any such modification. This structural fragility complicates the construction of [F][F]-irregular graphs compared to the classical case.

As far as we are aware, this work initiates the systematic investigation of [F][F]-irregularity, focusing on the canonical class of paths. Specifically, we completely solve the existence problem for [Pn][P_{n}]-irregular graphs posed in [4], and fully determine the possible orders of non-trivial [P3][P_{3}]-irregular graphs. Our main contributions are summarized in the following theorems.

Theorem 1.

For any path PnP_{n} of order n≥3n\geq 3, there exist infinitely many [Pn][P_{n}]-irregular graphs.

Theorem 2.

For an integer kk, a non-trivial [P3][P_{3}]-irregular graph of order kk exists if and only if k≥7k\geq 7.

Our approach is constructive: for each n≥3n\geq 3, we provide explicit families of graphs, determine the exact values of all [Pn][P_{n}]-degrees, and show that they are pairwise distinct.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the necessary preliminaries and notation. Section 3 is devoted to the proof of Theorem 2, characterizing [P3][P_{3}]-irregular graphs. Sections 4 and 5 focus on [P4][P_{4}]- and [P5][P_{5}]-irregularity, respectively. In Section 6, we settle the general case for all n≥6n\geq 6, thereby completing the proof of Theorem 1. Finally, Section 7 outlines the Strong Conjecture on [F][F]-irregular graphs.

2 Preliminaries

All numerical parameters in this paper are integers. Any set of indexed elements of the form {αx|i≤x≤j}\bigl\{\alpha_{x}\bigm|i\leq x\leq j\bigr\} is also written as {αi,…,αj}\{\alpha_{i},\dots,\alpha_{j}\}. For a graph GG, let V⁡(G)V(G) and E⁡(G)E(G) be its vertex and edge sets, respectively. The order of GG is |G|=|V⁡(G)||G|=|V(G)|, and GG is non-trivial if |G|≥2|G|\geq 2. An edge incident to vertices uu and vv is denoted by u​vuv. The degree of a vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) is the number of edges incident to vv, and GG is regular if all its vertices have the same degree. We use the notation KmK_{m} for the complete graph of order mm. A path PnP_{n} of order nn is a graph with V⁡(Pn)={u1,…,un}V(P_{n})=\{u_{1},\dots,u_{n}\} and E⁡(Pn)={ui​ui+1|1≤i≤n−1}E(P_{n})=\bigl\{u_{i}u_{i+1}\bigm|1\leq i\leq n-1\bigr\}. We write such a path as the vertex sequence u1​u2​…​unu_{1}u_{2}\dots u_{n}, where u1u_{1} and unu_{n} are called the end-vertices. If a graph contains a unique path with the end-vertices uu and vv, this path is denoted by u​…​vu\dots v; in particular, u​…​uu\dots u represents the single vertex uu. A graph is connected if every pair of its vertices is joined by a path.

A subgraph HH of GG is induced if E(H)={uv∈E(G)|u,v∈V(H)}E(H)=\bigl\{uv\in E(G)\bigm|u,v\in V(H)\bigr\}. For a vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), we denote by 𝒫n​(G,v)\mathcal{P}_{n}(G,v) the family of all induced subgraphs of GG isomorphic to PnP_{n} and containing vv. Consequently, the [Pn][P_{n}]-degree of a vertex vv in GG is exactly |𝒫n​(G,v)||\mathcal{P}_{n}(G,v)|.

3 On the order of [P3][P_{3}]-irregular graphs

We begin by introducing a parameterized family of graphs {G⁡(m,3)}m≥4\bigl\{G(m,3)\bigr\}_{m\geq 4}, where each graph has a corresponding odd order k=2​m+1k=2m+1.

Theorem 3.

For every integer m≥4m\geq 4, the graph G⁡(m,3)G(m,3) is [P3][P_{3}]-irregular.

Proof.

Fix an integer m≥4m\geq 4. Modulo mm, the vertex [P3][P_{3}]-degrees in G⁡(m,3)G(m,3) obtained in Lemma 1 split into four disjoint congruence classes

X\displaystyle X ≡1(modm),\displaystyle\equiv 1\pmod{m},
Am\displaystyle A_{m} ≡0(modm),\displaystyle\equiv 0\pmod{m},
Ai\displaystyle A_{i} ≡m−2(modm)for ​1≤i≤m−1,\displaystyle\equiv m-2\pmod{m}\quad\text{for }1\leq i\leq m-1,
Bj\displaystyle B_{j} ≡m−1(modm)for ​1≤j≤m.\displaystyle\equiv m-1\pmod{m}\quad\text{for }1\leq j\leq m.

This partition and the strict monotonicity of the sequences {Ai}i=1m−1\bigl\{A_{i}\bigr\}_{i=1}^{m-1} and {Bj}j=1m\bigl\{B_{j}\bigr\}_{j=1}^{m} imply that all these [P3][P_{3}]-degrees are pairwise distinct. Thus, G⁡(m,3)G(m,3) is [P3][P_{3}]-irregular. ∎

Corollary 1.

There exist infinitely many [P3][P_{3}]-irregular graphs.

3.2 Proof of Theorem 2

Recall that Theorem 2 states that a non-trivial [P3][P_{3}]-irregular graph of order kk exists if and only if k≥7k\geq 7.

Proof.

Necessity. To begin with, every [P3][P_{3}]-irregular graph is inherently asymmetric, i.e., its automorphism group is trivial. According to [6], there are no asymmetric graphs of orders 2≤k≤52\leq k\leq 5, and there are exactly eight such graphs of order 66, as shown in Figure 2. A direct check reveals that none of them is [P3][P_{3}]-irregular; there, in each graph, two vertices with the same [P3][P_{3}]-degree are marked with their equal values. Consequently, no [P3][P_{3}]-irregular graph exists for any order 2≤k≤62\leq k\leq 6. The necessity is proved.

Sufficiency. By Theorem 3, for each integer m≥4m\geq 4, the graph G⁡(m,3)G(m,3) of odd order k=2​m+1≥9k=2m+1\geq 9 is [P3][P_{3}]-irregular, and the exact formulae in Lemma 1 ensure that all its vertex [P3][P_{3}]-degrees are strictly positive. To complete the odd orders, Figure 3 depicts the [P3][P_{3}]-irregular graph G⁡(3,3)G(3,3) of order 77. It contains exactly 1616 induced subgraphs isomorphic to P3P_{3}: v1​v2​v3v_{1}v_{2}v_{3}, v1​v2​v6v_{1}v_{2}v_{6}, v1​v2​v7v_{1}v_{2}v_{7}, v1​v5​v3v_{1}v_{5}v_{3}, v1​v5​v6v_{1}v_{5}v_{6}; v2​v1​v5v_{2}v_{1}v_{5}, v2​v3​v4v_{2}v_{3}v_{4}, v2​v3​v5v_{2}v_{3}v_{5}, v2​v6​v5v_{2}v_{6}v_{5}; v3​v2​v6v_{3}v_{2}v_{6}, v3​v5​v6v_{3}v_{5}v_{6}, v3​v7​v6v_{3}v_{7}v_{6}; v4​v3​v5v_{4}v_{3}v_{5}, v4​v3​v7v_{4}v_{3}v_{7}; v5​v3​v7v_{5}v_{3}v_{7}, and v5​v6​v7v_{5}v_{6}v_{7}. Consequently, the [P3][P_{3}]-degrees of the vertices v1,…,v7v_{1},\dots,v_{7} in G⁡(3,3)G(3,3) are 6,8,10,3,9,76,8,10,3,9,7, and 55, respectively, which are also strictly positive.

A [P3][P_{3}]-irregular graph of every even order k≥8k\geq 8 can be constructed by adjoining an isolated vertex to G​(12​(k−2),3)G\left(\frac{1}{2}(k-2),3\right), thereby completing the proof of sufficiency. ∎

Theorem 4.

For every integer m≥7m\geq 7, the graph G⁡(m,4)G(m,4) is [P4][P_{4}]-irregular.

Proof.

Fix an integer m≥7m\geq 7. By Lemma 2, the sequence {Ai}i=1m−1\bigl\{A_{i}\bigr\}_{i=1}^{m-1} is strictly increasing with a maximum of Am−1=2​mA_{m-1}=2m and contains only even values, whereas {Bj}j=2m−1\bigl\{B_{j}\bigr\}_{j=2}^{m-1} is strictly decreasing with a maximum of B2=2​m−1B_{2}=2m-1 and comprises only odd values, ensuring that their terms are pairwise distinct. Moreover, we have the following chain of inequalities

2​m<Bm<Am<X1<X2<B1<Y1.2m<B_{m}<A_{m}<X_{1}<X_{2}<B_{1}<Y_{1}.

These arguments collectively demonstrate that all vertex [P4][P_{4}]-degrees in G⁡(m,4)G(m,4) are pairwise distinct, meaning that G⁡(m,4)G(m,4) is [P4][P_{4}]-irregular. ∎

Corollary 2.

For every integer k≥17k\geq 17, there exists a [P4][P_{4}]-irregular graph of order kk.

Proof.

For odd orders, the existence follows directly from Theorem 4. For any even order k≥18k\geq 18, the desired graph is obtained by adding an isolated vertex to the [P4][P_{4}]-irregular graph G​(12​(k−4),4)G\bigl(\frac{1}{2}(k-4),4\bigr) of odd order k−1k-1 having strictly positive vertex [P4][P_{4}]-degrees by Lemma 2. ∎

Theorem 5.

For every integer m≥7m\geq 7, the graph G⁡(m,5)G(m,5) is [P5][P_{5}]-irregular.

Fix an integer m≥7m\geq 7. Immediate inspection of Lemma 3 yields the strict ordering

Thus, the entries of these two sequences are pairwise distinct. Combined with the inequality B2<Am−1<Am=4​m−1B_{2}<A_{m-1}<A_{m}=4m-1, this implies that all the vertex [P5][P_{5}]-degrees in G⁡(m,5)G(m,5) are pairwise distinct, confirming that G⁡(m,5)G(m,5) is [P5][P_{5}]-irregular. ∎

Analogously to the proof of Corollary 2, we obtain the following result.

Corollary 3.

For every integer k≥19k\geq 19, there exists a [P5][P_{5}]-irregular graph of order kk.

Lemma 11.

If n=7n=7 with m≡1(mod6)m\equiv 1\pmod{6}, or n≠7n\neq 7 with m≡3(modn−1)m\equiv 3\pmod{n-1}, then

{X1,Y1}∩{Ai,Bj}=∅for all ​1≤i≤m−1​ and ​2≤j≤m−1.\{X_{1},Y_{1}\}\cap\{A_{i},B_{j}\}=\emptyset\qquad\text{for all }1\leq i\leq m-1\text{ and }2\leq j\leq m-1.
Proof.

For each admissible pair (i,j)(i,j), we show that any two [Pn][P_{n}]-degrees from distinct sets {X1,Y1}\{X_{1},Y_{1}\} and {Ai,Bj}\{A_{i},B_{j}\} have incongruent residues modulo n−1n-1.

Indeed, by Lemmas 4–7, we have

Y1−Ai\displaystyle Y_{1}-A_{i} =5​m−9−i⁡(n−1)≡5​m−9(modn−1),\displaystyle=5m-9-i(n-1)\equiv 5m-9\pmod{n-1},

If n=7n=7 and m≡1(mod6)m\equiv 1\pmod{6}, these differences yield the non-zero residues 5,1,2,4(mod6)5,1,2,4\pmod{6}, respectively. Hence, the assertion follows. ∎

Theorem 6.

For all integers n≥6n\geq 6 and m≥2​nm\geq 2n satisfying either n=7n=7 with m≡1(mod6)m\equiv 1\pmod{6}, or n≠7n\neq 7 with m≡3(modn−1)m\equiv 3\pmod{n-1}, the graph G⁡(m,n)G(m,n) is [Pn][P_{n}]-irregular.

Proof.

By Lemmas 9–12, all vertex [Pn][P_{n}]-degrees in G⁡(m,n)G(m,n) are pairwise distinct. This immediately implies that G⁡(m,n)G(m,n) is [Pn][P_{n}]-irregular. ∎

Corollary 4.

For every integer n≥6n\geq 6, there exist infinitely many [Pn][P_{n}]-irregular graphs.

By Corollaries 1–4, the assertion of Theorem 1 holds.

7 Conclusion

This paper provides the first structural results on [F][F]-irregularity. For any path PnP_{n} of order n≥3n\geq 3, we explicitly constructed infinite families of graphs with pairwise distinct vertex [Pn][P_{n}]-degrees, and established that the order kk of a non-trivial [P3][P_{3}]-irregular graph can be any integer k≥7k\geq 7 and no other. These results prompt us to formulate the following conjecture.

Conjecture 3 (Strong Conjecture about [F][F]-irregular graphs).

For every connected graph FF of order |F|≥3|F|\geq 3, there exist infinitely many [F][F]-irregular graphs.

A natural next step is to extend the concept of [F][F]-irregularity to oriented graphs, as was recently done for classical FF-irregularity [7]. First and foremost, we pose the existence problem for [F][F]-irregular oriented graphs where FF is a directed path or a directed cycle, both of order n≥3n\geq 3.
